idiom_name: AtomicReference CAS loop over an immutable state record
implementation_notes: The JDK has no STM, and the closest things are not it: `java.util.concurrent.locks` gives you mutual exclusion, `java.util.concurrent.atomic` gives you single-location CAS, and `synchronized` gives you the simplest possible coarse lock. Two structural facts make the manual form workable in Java specifically: the GC means snapshots can be reference copies of immutable objects rather than deep copies, and `java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference` (or `AtomicStampedReference` when you need ABA protection) makes publish-and-detect a single instruction. So the realisation is the same shape as everywhere else - hold the shared state in an `AtomicReference<State>` where State is an immutable record, read it, compute a new State, `compareAndSet` it, and on failure re-read and replay. For anything larger, `StampedLock` with optimistic reads gets you most of the snapshot behaviour with a fraction of the complexity, at the cost of no atomicity across several reads. Java's type system also enforces the pattern's most important precondition better than most languages: making the shared state class immutable and the mutable holder `private final` means no reference outside the holder can mutate what the read set recorded.
pitfalls: Calling state.get() more than once inside the block and reading different fields from different snapshots, which is a torn read the CAS loop cannot detect.
Using AtomicStampedReference unnecessarily and paying the extra stamp; it exists to defeat ABA, and an immutable state object with a monotonic version defeats it more cheaply.
Retrying with the stale `cur` after a failed CAS instead of re-reading, which loops forever without making progress.
Making State mutable (mutable fields in a class held by AtomicReference) so that the snapshot reference silently changes under the transaction.
synchronized on several locks in different orders across call sites - the deadlock class STM removes.
